newsitem.title: USA: IMF official calls for small rise in U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: IMF official calls for small rise in U.S. rates.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official called on the Federal Reserve to tighten credit but saw no need now for further cuts in German interest rates.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television and at a news conference, IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer also said that the Japanese recovery was "well underway" and forecast growth there next year of 2.7 percent.
Fischer was generally upbeat about the outlook for the world economy as a whole. "It looks reasonably good," he said. "We see very low inflation in the G7 (Group of Seven) countries."

Economic growth in the United States has "strengthened quite a bit. It's probably about time for a rise in interest rates," the IMF official said. Asked if a substantial rate increase was needed, he replied, "it doesn't seem to be necessary right now."
The U.S. central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on September 24 to plot monetary strategy and some analysts are betting it will tighten credit at that time.
Fischer was encouraged by the Bundesbank's recent sharp cut in German interest rates, saying it had "really made a difference." "We don't see a need right now for any further easing," he said.

But he made clear that Germany and its European counterparts needed to monitor the situation closely as they strive to meet the tough budget goals set out in the Maastricht treaty for the launch of European Monetary Union.
"If the situation were to slow or not develop as well as we hoped, there would be a case for a further easing," he said.
Fischer signalled out Europe as one potential trouble spot for the world economy in 1997.

"If there would be difficulties, they could be associated with the possibility that the growth we see for Europe does not happen," the senior IMF official said. "The combination of the need to meet the Maastricht criteria and growth might create policy dilemmas there."
Fischer sounded a more optimistic note about Japan, which until recently had been mired in a virtual recession. "The Japanese recovery now seems to be well underway," he said.
He said the IMF expects Japan's economy to grow about 2.7 percent next year.
That forecast assumes that Tokyo will introduce a supplementary budget this fall, but it is expected to be a much smaller than last year.

Japan's economy has been aided by a steep depreciation of the yen against the dollar over the last 1-1/2 years, brought on in part by foreign exchange market intervention by Tokyo and to a lesser extent, Washington. The dollar has also risen against European currencies, but less markedly.

In its 1996 annual report released on Thursday, the IMF said the dollar's rally has brought currency rates "to levels more consistent with fundamentals." But, reporting on one of its board discussions in September 1995, it said IMF directors cautioned countries against relying too heavily on intervention to influence exchange rates.

Elsewhere in the world economy, the IMF expects the so- called transition economies of the former communist bloc to register "positive growth" on the whole for the first time since the break-up of the Soviet Union.
"Growth in Africa is picking up," Fischer added. "Growth in Latin America is picking up."
Economic growth in East Asian nations is expected to slow in 1997, but to levels -- seven, eight, nine percent -- that would still be regarded as a "gallop" elsewhere in the world, he added.
